title: The Gaza Plan Dies, Hormuz Escalates, and a Stretched US Navy Shows the Strain
subhead: Netanyahu's rejection of the US-backed Gaza disarmament plan killed the conflict's only diplomatic framework weeks before Israeli elections, while the Hormuz standoff hardened — Trump vowing to declare the strait US territory as shipping traffic collapsed to a fraction of pre-war levels. Across the same week, the human and material costs of a prolonged war and a warming climate accumulated: a carrier crew at the breaking point, interceptor stockpiles down 65 percent, and two major earthquakes in a week.

sections.heading: The Gaza Peace Plan Collapses Under Netanyahu's Rejection
sections.body:
The week opened with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu formally rejecting the US-backed 15-point Gaza disarmament plan at a cabinet meeting, declaring Israel 'will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed' and dismissing the framework as offering 'fictitious disarmament'. The rejection derailed the most serious diplomatic effort to resolve the Gaza conflict since the October 2025 ceasefire — a plan under which Hamas had accepted a phased disarmament process in exchange for an Israeli withdrawal and the creation of a Palestinian National Committee to govern Gaza.

The White House appeared unbothered, with a senior US official telling Israeli journalist Barak Ravid that 'we understand Bibi's political needs' — framing the rejection as campaign rhetoric ahead of Israel's 27 October general election, the first since the 7 October attacks. Former Israeli diplomat Alon Pinkas told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu 'needs a forever war' and that the rejection 'should be viewed entirely in the context of the upcoming election'. Far-right ministers including Itamar Ben Gvir have pressured Netanyahu to scrap the deal entirely.

By Friday, the administration was moving to rescue the framework: Jared Kushner, Board of Peace high representative Nickolay Mladenov, and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair were due in Israel on Sunday before traveling to Cairo. Construction of the first International Stabilisation Force base in Rafah is still scheduled to begin this month. The gap between Hamas's acceptance and Israel's insistence on full disarmament before any withdrawal remains the central unresolved tension.
sections.whyItMatters: The most credible path out of the Gaza conflict is now a dead letter, hostage to Israeli election politics. Whether Kushner's high-level visit can revive it will determine whether Gaza has any diplomatic route forward — and whether Washington can claim a foreign-policy win before US midterms.

sections.heading: Hormuz Hardens: Trump's 'US Territory' Threat as Shipping Collapses
sections.body:
The Strait of Hormuz standoff escalated sharply over the week. On Saturday, President Donald Trump said he will 'soon' declare the strait a US territory — a unilateral territorial claim over an international waterway that would be a major legal and diplomatic rupture. The rhetoric had been building all week: Trump insisted the US has 'total control' over the strait and called the blockade of Iranian ports 'A WALL OF STEEL', while demanding Iran pay war reparations for '50 years' of damage, including the 2000 USS Cole bombing.

The reality on the water tells a different story. Just eight ships transited the strait on Tuesday, far below the 130 to 140 that crossed daily before the war, according to Reuters citing Kpler. Iran's new security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said the strait will not reopen until the US ends the war and blockade, releases frozen assets, and agrees to a region-wide ceasefire including Lebanon and Gaza. The US military fired two Hellfire missiles at a Panama-flagged vessel attempting to run the blockade, disabling its steering gear — the latest in a campaign that has redirected 55 vessels, disabled three, and boarded two.

Two UAE tankers were hit by drones while transiting the strait on Friday, and the first confirmed Houthi shipping deaths of the war came midweek when a double-tap strike on the cargo vessel Tihamah in the Bab al-Mandeb killed at least six crew and rescuers. Analysts, including Dennis Citrinowicz of the Institute for National Security Studies, warned that the drive to frame the conflict as a victory is creating a 'virtual reality' that prevents decisions based on the situation on the ground.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between Washington's claims of control and the reality of near-empty shipping lanes is widening into a credibility problem. A formal US territorial claim over Hormuz would be a rupture with international law and every Gulf state, and the strait's closure continues to weigh on global energy prices and inflation.

sections.heading: A Stretched US Military Shows the Strain
sections.body:
Three developments this week exposed how the Iran war is consuming US military capacity faster than it can be rebuilt. First, the Pentagon ordered defence firms to submit plans within 21 days for 'significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules' on critical weapons. The urgency is driven by hard numbers: CSIS analysis shows US Patriot interceptor stockpiles have fallen from 2,330 to between 759 and 827 — a reduction of at least 65 percent — with THAAD interceptors down 38 percent. Retired Marine Corps colonel Mark Cancian warned: 'If we run out of Patriots, then the missiles get through.'

Second, the crew-welfare crisis aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln — more than 250 days at sea with reported food shortages, broken plumbing, and sailors attempting to jump overboard — triggered a Senate inquiry. Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal asked Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth whether the Navy 'can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force'. Hegseth dismissed the reports as 'completely misrepresented'. The USS George Washington is now departing to relieve the Lincoln, pulling the last US carrier out of the Pacific.

Third, Iraq's Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi declared the September 30 deadline for ending the US-led coalition's military mission 'fixed and final', closing a US presence that began with the 2003 invasion. And in a separate, ideologically driven move, Trump ordered the Navy to rip out the electromagnetic catapults on its newest Ford-class carriers and return to steam — a costly rollback at a moment of acute naval strain, and a widening gap with China and France, whose newest carriers use electromagnetic systems.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is managing a widening set of commitments — Iran, the Red Sea, the Pacific, Europe — with shrinking stockpiles, a fatigued carrier force, and a shrinking regional footprint. The carrier pullout from the Pacific comes just as China shows more assertiveness in the South China Sea, raising questions about Washington's ability to reassure allies on multiple fronts at once.

sections.heading: Two Earthquakes in a Week Test New and Strained Governments
sections.body:
Two major earthquakes struck within six days, both in the Pacific Ring of Fire. On Monday, a magnitude 7.4 quake hit western Colombia, killing at least 132 people and injuring more than 480, with the worst damage in Pereira and Cali where dozens of buildings collapsed. The disaster landed on Colombia's newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella — who took office only the previous Friday — forcing him to declare a national disaster and grant special powers to reallocate budgets just days into his presidency.

On Saturday, a magnitude 7.7 quake struck off Indonesia's Flores region at a shallow 10km depth, killing at least 47 people and toppling buildings in East Nusa Tenggara, with the toll expected to rise as search-and-rescue operations continue. The shallow depth and proximity to populated coastal towns made this one particularly destructive, raising the risk of landslides and a possible tsunami threat.

The two disasters bookend a week in which the human cost of both conflict and climate accumulated across the board: a sanctioned-oil spill from the tanker Caroline Bezengi reached Oman's coastline covering more than 2,000 square kilometres, and record-low Danube water levels forced Romania to take its only nuclear plant offline for at least 10 days.
sections.whyItMatters: Both quakes test governments already under strain — Colombia's brand-new president and an Indonesia repeatedly hit by natural disasters. They are a reminder that the week's geopolitical crises are unfolding against a backdrop of compounding climate and disaster risk that no administration can fully control.

sections.heading: The Middle East Realigns Even as Its Wars Grind On
sections.body:
Beneath the headlines about Gaza and Hormuz, the region's political map shifted in significant ways. Syria's new government sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes — a largely symbolic verdict given his exile in Russia, but a formal break with the Assad era and a milestone for transitional justice. Damascus also reached a deal to convert Russia's two military bases into 'joint training and capacity-building centres', a quiet downgrading of Moscow's Middle East footprint on terms set by Syria, not Russia.

Lebanon became the first Middle Eastern country to abolish the death penalty, passing the legislation over Hezbollah's opposition — a striking rights achievement in the midst of regional war. Yet the same week, Israeli air strikes killed at least 11 people in southern Lebanon, and Hezbollah urged the government to abandon what it called 'humiliating' direct negotiations, threatening to unravel the fragile ceasefire and US-mediated border talks.

Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Egypt could join the Turkey-Saudi-Pakistan Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, a collective-deterrence pact signed the previous Friday that analysts have compared to NATO's Article 5. Expanding the pact to include Egypt would significantly broaden a new Middle East security bloc at a time when the US-Iran war is reshaping regional alignments. And in Latin America, Venezuela restored consular ties with Israel after 17 years, the latest domino in a right-wing realignment across the continent.
sections.whyItMatters: Even as the Gaza and Hormuz conflicts resist resolution, the region is consolidating into new blocs and new legal norms — a post-Assad Syria asserting sovereignty, a Lebanon abolishing capital punishment, and a Turkey-led defence pact potentially expanding. These shifts may outlast the current wars and define the region's next order.

sections.heading: Ukraine Deepens Its Strike Reach as Russia Closes Political Space
sections.body:
Ukraine demonstrated a growing domestic strike capability this week, hitting targets deep inside Russia. A drone strike on Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan — over 1,100km from the border — killed at least 13 people, including seven Uzbek citizens, targeting the Tanevo oil refinery owned by Tatneft. A massive overnight attack on the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk killed three people and hit grain terminals, threatening global wheat supplies. And on Saturday, Ukraine used domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles to strike a military airfield and the Progress Centre rocket facility in Samara that supports Russia's Starlink-style satellite internet network.

Kyiv also handed Washington new proposals to end the four-and-a-half-year war, focused on strengthening Ukraine's air defences and increasing pressure on Moscow. Zelenskyy accused Russia of planning to use next month's parliamentary elections as a pretext for a new mobilisation of 'several hundred thousand' troops by year's end. Moscow, meanwhile, is demanding answers from Washington and Ankara about a potential plan to send Kyiv a 'substantial arsenal' of US weapons and ammunition held by Turkey.

On the political front, a Moscow court barred Yabloko, Russia's only registered anti-war party, from standing in next month's parliamentary elections — eliminating the last organised opposition voice from the ballot and virtually guaranteeing a Kremlin-friendly Duma even as United Russia's ratings have fallen to 33 percent amid inflation and drone strikes.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine is proving it can strike Russia's industrial and communications heartland with its own weapons, disrupting oil revenue and satellite infrastructure that fund the war — while Russia closes off the last peaceful outlet for opposition. The war is entering a phase of deeper mutual escalation with no diplomatic track in sight.

bottomLine: This was the week the Gaza peace plan died and the Hormuz standoff hardened into open escalation — Trump vowing to declare an international strait US territory even as shipping traffic collapsed to eight vessels a day and the first Houthi shipping deaths of the war occurred. The through-line is a US military stretched across Iran, the Red Sea, and the Pacific with interceptor stockpiles down 65 percent, a carrier crew at the breaking point, and a September 30 withdrawal from Iraq locked in. The costs of prolonged conflict and a warming climate are accumulating faster than leaders can manage them: two major earthquakes in a week, a sanctioned-oil spill reaching Oman's coast, and a European drought forcing a nuclear plant offline. Going forward, the questions that matter are whether Kushner can revive the Gaza framework, whether Trump's Hormuz rhetoric becomes policy, and whether a US focused on the Western Hemisphere can reassure allies in a Pacific it has just left without a carrier.
sources: Al Jazeera, BBC, AP, Reuters, Washington Post, CSIS, Guardian, Israel Democracy Institute, EU Copernicus, USGS, Indonesian BASARNAS, Oman News Agency
